target: AG1’s claim that AI makes everyday life more enjoyable and convenient; improves health and standard of living; makes work easier; helps marginalized groups; and improves workplace safety, leading to AI being good for society.
objection: AI can automate or replicate human work in ways that reduce labor demand and shift value toward owners of the technology, so AI can harm the economic well-being of many workers and businesses.

target: AG1’s claim that AI is broadly beneficial for people’s lives and should be viewed positively overall.
objection: When people rely on AI outputs for answers and decisions, it can weaken independent reasoning and reduce learning of underlying concepts, undermining critical thinking in students and adults.

target: AG1’s positive assessment of AI’s social effects.
objection: AI models can learn from biased data and reproduce or amplify discriminatory patterns, so AI can hurt racial minorities by repeating and exacerbating racism.

target: AG1’s positive assessment of AI’s social effects.
objection: AI systems often require collecting, linking, and processing personal or sensitive data, which creates dangerous privacy risks.

target: AG1’s claim that responsible development and governance can substantially reduce AI harms.
objection: The harms AI creates are structurally tied to scale: firms deploy AI to automate and cut labor costs, models reproduce patterns from large datasets, and AI use requires extensive personal data collection that can still leak or be inferred despite controls. Therefore, society-wide elimination of these harms is not realistically achievable just through governance.

target: AG1’s claim that safeguards can substantially mitigate AI harms.
objection: The proposed safeguards may reduce some harms, but they do not remove the underlying structural drivers of labor disruption, discrimination, and privacy loss across all deployments and time horizons, so the harms persist at meaningful levels.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can be net positive if harms are mitigated.
objection: The harms to economic well-being, critical thinking, racial equality, and privacy are highly important because they directly affect opportunities, autonomy, and civil rights, so persistent harms can outweigh welfare gains overall.

target: AG1’s claim that AI benefits outweigh harms overall.
objection: In real deployments, AI’s benefits are unevenly distributed while displacement risk, biased errors, and privacy exposure fall on broader groups, so AI cannot be expected to be good for society overall.

target: AG1’s claim that AI’s everyday assistance, health, work, accessibility, and safety benefits outweigh its downsides.
objection: There is substantial documented evidence that AI creates significant harms to workers, racial minorities, and the public through job substitution, discriminatory impacts, and privacy loss.

target: AG1’s claim that AI benefits and harms are not systematically skewed against society overall.
objection: AI’s welfare gains do not automatically neutralize the harms at society-wide scale, because displaced workers, unequal harms, and privacy exposures remain unless structural remedies truly work, and mitigation is uneven across contexts and time horizons.

target: AG1’s claim that improvements in health, workplace safety, and accessibility can outweigh harms.
objection: Persistent harms do not automatically imply AI is not good for society, but because health and safety are major drivers of quality of life and economic well-being, gains in those areas do not erase the broader social importance of the harms.

target: AG1’s claim that the inability to eliminate every harm does not mean AI cannot be socially good.
objection: AG1’s argument wrongly assumes that if harms cannot be perfectly eliminated, AI can still be called good overall; AG2 objects that the inability to eliminate every harm does not by itself settle the issue in AI’s favor.

target: AG1’s claim that AI’s welfare gains across daily life, health, disability access, and workplace safety are enough to support a positive social judgment.
objection: Even if AI improves several welfare dimensions, society should not judge AI as good overall if the harms to many people’s quality of life remain substantial.

target: AG1’s claim that widely available AI tooling keeps competition open and prevents concentration.
objection: Lowering barriers to build AI applications does not stop winner-take-most outcomes when dominant firms still control key bottlenecks such as distribution, major customer access, and the ability to scale cheaply through concentrated infrastructure and data assets.

target: AG1’s claim that competitive entry can remain viable and prevent concentration of AI power.
objection: Winner-take-most concentration can still occur even when many developers can build AI apps, so open tooling does not prove that AI power will be broadly distributed.

target: AG1’s claim that competitive entry and distributed access mean AI benefits will be broadly shared rather than concentrated.
objection: If dominance persists through concentrated value-capture bottlenecks, welfare gains like convenience, health, and safety are less likely to reach workers and smaller businesses, while displacement and leverage losses still fall widely; therefore broad welfare gains do not imply AI is good for society overall.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy-preserving methods and legal remedies can prevent AI privacy harms.
objection: Effective AI deployment usually requires collecting and linking sensitive data at scale, and competition creates incentives to gather and reuse even more data; as data scale and linkability increase, privacy leakage and harmful inference remain meaningful even with competitive entry.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy risks can be effectively prevented or greatly reduced in practice.
objection: Privacy harms undermine autonomy and equal participation, so they count strongly against AI being good for society overall, and AG1’s welfare gains do not show these harms are largely avoided or outweighed.

target: AG1’s claim that broad welfare gains across health, safety, accessibility, and productivity can offset economic harms from concentration.
objection: Economic insecurity from job displacement, wage suppression, and weaker bargaining power worsens health and safety outcomes too, so AI-related labor-market harm can offset the very welfare domains that AI is said to improve.

target: AG1’s claim that AI’s health/work/safety gains are sufficient to show it is good overall.
objection: AI deployment tends to concentrate market power, which increases economic insecurity for many workers and small businesses; when bargaining power and alternatives shrink, those harms can spill into health and safety, so the claimed welfare gains are not sufficient to establish that AI is good for society overall.
